claim: Production choice by noisy utility U=P*G-C with softmax noise (t about 0.5) is the textbook ACT-R rule; P is learned from success/failure counts, C from effort.
agent_test: Give each operator a Beta success count and mean token cost; pick by softmax(P*G-C). Compare with fixed order at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: People shift strategy by experience. Lovett and Anderson 1995 (N=67 analysed, 90 problems) found most chose the more successful strategy and overmatched, and a Bayesian-posterior ACT-R model with Gaussian noise variance 0.05^2 (SD 0.05) fit R2=.99 in aggregate but only .66 for individuals' last-45-problem selections. Xie and Moss 2025 (N=100) replicated the related Lovett and Schunn 1999 result. The 1996 journal paper was still not opened; the 'over 80% chose overshoot on problem 5' detail comes from a 2006 chapter.
agent_test: Make a task family where operator A stops working mid-stream; measure trials to switch under utility vs fixed order.
audit_note: Lovett and Anderson set the Gaussian noise variance to 0.05 squared (0.0025, SD 0.05), not 0.052; the .99 and .66 R2 values, 68 subjects with 1 removed, and 90 problems check out (page says eight conditions, not four).
claim_before_audit: People shift strategy by experience. Lovett and Anderson 1995 (N=67, 90 problems) found most chose the more successful strategy and overmatched, and a Bayesian-posterior ACT-R model with noise variance 0.052 fit R2=.99 in aggregate but only .66 for individuals. Xie and Moss 2025 (N=100) replicated the related Lovett and Schunn 1999 result. The 1996 journal paper was still not opened; the 'over 80% chose overshoot on problem 5' detail comes from a 2006 chapter.

claim: People pick the cheaper information strategy in proportion to time cost; the model with t=0.491 picks the faster of two strategies 88.5% of the time at a 1 s difference. Gray 2006: 3 experiments, 16-18 per cell, linear cost trend explained 98% of condition variance.
agent_test: Vary per-operator token cost; check that the agent shifts to cheaper operators at the predicted rate.

claim: Utility noise is a free parameter, not a constant: about 0.5 by convention in ACT-R, 0.491 fitted in Gray et al. 2006, and 0.440 (with learning rate alpha 0.759) in a single-participant likelihood fit in Stocco et al. 2024.
agent_test: Sweep softmax temperature at equal tokens; report sensitivity.
audit_note: Sources confirm 0.5 convention (Taatgen), 0.491 fitted (Gray 2006) and alpha 0.759 / noise 0.440 for one participant (Stocco), but noise 0.440 is close to 0.5 and 0.491, so 'very different procedural model' is not supported for the noise; only alpha and the single-participant fit differ.
claim_before_audit: Utility noise is a free parameter, not a constant: 0.5 by convention, 0.491 fitted in Gray 2006, and a one-participant fit gave a very different procedural model (alpha 0.759, noise 0.440).

claim: The ACT-R utility rule is a Rescorla-Wagner-style reinforcement learning update with credit for multi-step sequences handled by time-discounted shared reward; Fu and Anderson (2004) extended it with temporal-difference learning, and one human ERP study (Walsh and Anderson 2011) found TD models with eligibility traces fit best.
agent_test: Compare end-of-episode reward sharing vs discounted TD credit for operator sequences.
audit_note: Gall and Fruehwirth confirm ACT-R's difference-rule utility update with time-discounted shared reward; but 'neural work favours TD with eligibility traces' rests on one human ERP study (Walsh & Anderson 2011, from the ACT-R lab; its BIC comparison could not be re-opened because PMC blocked the full text), and Fu & Anderson 2004 shows ACT-R already has a TD extension.
claim_before_audit: The utility rule is a form of reinforcement learning, but credit assignment over multi-step sequences is heuristic in ACT-R; neural work favours TD models with eligibility traces.

claim: Tabular RL of production selection learns small tasks but does not scale: 12 steps by about 5,000 episodes, 18 steps by 9,000, 34-step task needed about 22,000 episodes and still left 6 of 24 nonsense states.
agent_test: Need many episodes per operator context; use coarse contexts (few states) in the agent.

claim: Utility learning assumes reward seeking; people who stay after punishment fit poorly (joint L 0.028 vs 0.007, still poor).
agent_test: Test operator stats using success only vs success and failure asymmetric weighting.

claim: In an LLM agent (Zhu and Simmons 2024) ACT-R style utility reuse of learned rules matched action-only LLM on success (15/15 vs 14-15/15) with no significant step difference. No ablation of utility vs random choice exists. Update: MACLA (d05) shows Bayesian success selection beats similarity-only ranking by 7.8 to 9.1 points, still no random or fixed-order control.
agent_test: Ablate: utility choice vs random vs fixed order among rules, equal tokens.

claim: Ignoring quit outcomes (no negative update) is a deliberate design to avoid punishing impossible tasks.
agent_test: Test negative update on abandon vs none.

claim: Off-the-shelf LLMs explore badly in context: GPT-4 basic prompt had suffix failure in over 60% of replicates; only 1 of 72 configurations (summary, suggestive hint, CoT) succeeded.
agent_test: Keep success counts outside the model and show a per-operator summary instead of raw history.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: External summaries/algorithmic support help large models: Gemini Pro MAB win-rate 45.5 raw, 60.0 summarized, 59.6 algorithm-guided, UCB 90.6; small Gemma models did not benefit (10.5 to 5.3 and 4.1).
agent_test: Provide per-operator win/cost table in prompt; compare with raw log on a strong and a weak model.

claim: LLM-based bandit routing across strategies/tools beats random: 76.7% vs 49.0% (30 queries per mode, no CI); 7.2% and 7.27% net reward gain in model selection pipelines.
agent_test: Run Thompson sampling over operators with real feedback; at least 100 items, give CIs.

claim: LLMs learn with an optimism bias when they choose the option themselves: positive learning rate 0.87 vs negative 0.10 (Claude v1.3, 50 runs); the bias reverses for foregone outcomes and disappears when someone else chooses. GPT-3 was human-like on the short-horizon bandit but below human on decisions from descriptions. Whether success counts kept by a scaffold would avoid the bias is an untested hypothesis.
agent_test: Compare model-estimated vs scaffold-counted operator success; measure asymmetry.
audit_note: Numbers check out (Claude v1.3 0.87 vs 0.10, GPT-3 horizon/descriptions results), but no source tests scaffold-kept success counts; the optimism bias is also reported only when the model chose the option itself (it reverses for foregone outcomes and vanishes when another agent chooses).
claim_before_audit: LLMs learn with an optimism bias: positive learning rate 0.87 vs negative 0.10 (Claude v1.3, 50 runs); GPT-3 was human-like in short-horizon bandit but below human on descriptions. Success counts kept by scaffold avoid this bias.

claim: Fine-tuning an LLM toward ACT-R traces (LLM-ACTR) gives hold-out accuracy 0.6576 vs chance 0.4826 and Llama 0.3564 on a simulated agent; a reviewer called gains minuscule. Training, not scaffold.
agent_test: Not applicable for a scaffold-only agent.

claim: Task-subtask utility (similarity-based) correlates with success: 14.0% to 24.5% across bins, Spearman 0.98; correlational and not outcome-based. Update: the paper (arXiv 2608.20274v2) is verified; whole-task skills lowered average success by 1.2 (text) and 4.1 (code) points, subtask skills raised it by 1.9 and 0.5.
agent_test: Compute outcome-based utility, check calibration against bins.

claim: Skill saving and reuse cuts tokens up to 80% but errors compound when skills nest.
agent_test: Count tokens with and without reuse at fixed accuracy.

claim: The two ACT-R utility formulations (success/cost vs reward difference) differ in tie-breaking and give different final utilities in the same toy game.
agent_test: Make tie-breaking explicit (random) in the operator selector.

claim: Learned success-posterior selection of procedures beats similarity-only retrieval in an LLM agent: ALFWorld Llama-2-7B 79.4/81.2 without it vs 87.2/90.3 with it (seen/unseen), reuse 62% vs 78%. Control is similarity, not random or fixed order; procedures are skills not reasoning operators.
agent_test: Ablate success-posterior choice vs random vs fixed order among reasoning operators at equal tokens.

claim: Per-step choice of reasoning depth beats every fixed depth: CogRouter (trained) 92.5% at 1,739 tokens vs fixed L1 76.5% at 357 and fixed L4 86.5% at 4,641 (ALFWorld, Qwen2.5-7B). Training-based; no counts rule and no random-choice control.
agent_test: Compare counts-based operator choice to fixed-depth and random-depth controls at equal tokens.

claim: Failure penalties can collapse the router to the cheapest operator: CogRouter with failed trajectories reweighted too fell to 83.0% and 83.1% of steps at the lightest level; without balanced cold start it collapsed to one level (86.0%).
agent_test: Cap the negative update and keep minimum exploration per operator.

claim: Decayed counts handle operator drift: geometric forgetting (0.997 per step) recovered reward to 0.8630 vs 0.8850 before a silent 18% quality drop (20 seeds, CI), and adopted a new arm within 142 steps. Proposed sliding window 50 / forgetting 0.95 in another paper is untested. Arms were models, not reasoning operators.
agent_test: Break one operator mid-stream; compare no decay, gamma 0.95 and gamma 0.99 on trials to switch.

claim: Cold start: informed priors and warm starts help. Removing a 5-query warm start cost 5.5 points (71.2 vs 76.7, 30 queries); MACLA reached 45% with 20% of the data and 82% with 50%. Prior strength was never swept.
agent_test: Sweep prior pseudo-counts (for example 2, 5, 20, 255) and report accuracy after 5, 20, 50 observations per context.

claim: LLM self-estimates of success are inflated and do not recover after failures: predicted 77% when true 22% (Gemini, SWE-bench Pro, N=100); all models stayed above 0.5 predicted success when failing 50% (512 contract sequences); only some models learn to decline.
agent_test: Compare scaffold counts to model-rated operator success; if model rating is used, use adversarial framing.
audit_note: Kaddour's 77% / 22% is a post-execution estimate (Gemini pre-execution mean 99%); Barkan shows predicted success stays above 0.5 but does fall with in-context failures, so 'do not recover' means 'stay overconfident'.

claim: Skill sharing across tasks is not safe by default: whole-task skills lowered success (-1.2 text, -4.1 code points) and one run fell 27.3% to 1.0%; subtask-level sharing helped slightly (+1.9, +0.5). Outcome-based shared utility is untested.
agent_test: Share operator statistics at subtask grain and compare with a no-memory control.

claim: Credit assignment for sequences: humans' single-step choices are fit by a TD-extended ACT-R rule (a=0.1, K=1.0, R2 0.94 to 0.98); the 2006 sequence paper says implicit learning worked only with distinct state information (abstract only, not opened). No test on reasoning-operator sequences.
agent_test: Compare end-of-episode equal credit vs discounted credit on 3-step operator chains.

claim: LLMs left to pick arms explore badly: TextBandit best-arm rate Qwen3-4B 89.2% but Qwen3-8B 37.5%, Llama-3.1-8B 31.6%, Phi-2 25.4% vs Thompson 51.1%, random 31.8%; in changing tasks LLMs show weak directed exploration even with thinking. Scaffold should own temperature and uncertainty bonus.
agent_test: Keep the selector outside the model; decay temperature over time.
